title: Composite Pattern
oneLiner: Lets you treat a single object and a whole tree of objects through the exact same interface.

hero.name: Nestor
hero.catchphrase: One leaf, one branch, one interface.
hero.power: Treats individual objects and entire nested groups of them identically, so tree structures can be processed recursively with no special cases.
hero.weakness: Because leaves and branches share one interface, it's hard to stop someone from calling 'add child' on something that was only ever meant to be a leaf.
hero.origin: Nestor formed after a file-explorer's render function needed one code path for `File` and a totally different one for `Folder`, doubling every feature added.

story.problem: Rendering a file explorer means checking `if (item instanceof File) ... else if (item instanceof Folder) { for (const child of item.children) ... }` — every new feature needs both branches written and kept in sync.
story.solution: Nestor gives File and Folder the same `FileSystemItem` interface, with `getSize()`. Folder's implementation just sums its children's `getSize()` — files and folders become interchangeable to the caller.
story.result: Rendering, sizing, and searching all become one recursive function with zero type-checking, whether the item is a single file or a folder nested ten levels deep.

before: Every feature needs a File branch and a Folder branch
instanceof checks scattered through the codebase
Adding a new item type means updating every branch everywhere
after: One interface, one recursive function, no branches
Files and folders are fully interchangeable to callers
A new item type just implements the shared interface

panels.label: The Problem
panels.caption: getTotalSize() has an instanceof File branch and a separate instanceof Folder branch that loops over children.
panels.speaker: Developer
panels.dialogue: I just added a third place with this exact same File-vs-Folder branching. There has to be a better way.

panels.label: The Hero Arrives
panels.caption: Nestor arrives holding a set of nesting dolls, each one opening to reveal another.
panels.speaker: Nestor
panels.dialogue: Stop treating leaves and branches differently. Give them the SAME interface — then one function handles both, forever.

panels.label: Pattern Power
panels.caption: File and Folder both implement getSize(). Folder's getSize() just sums its children's getSize().
panels.speaker: Nestor
panels.dialogue: Call getSize() on anything — a single file or a folder nested ten levels deep. The recursion just... works.

panels.label: The Result
panels.caption: getTotalSize(), render(), and search() are each a single, branch-free function.
panels.speaker: Developer
panels.dialogue: Three functions went from 40 branching lines each to one clean recursive call. No more instanceof anywhere.

useWhen: Your data is naturally tree-shaped (file systems, UI component trees, org charts, menu structures) with individual items and groups of items.
You want client code to treat a single object and a composite of objects identically.
Operations (size, render, search) need to apply recursively across the whole tree with no special-casing.
avoidWhen: The structure is flat — there's no meaningful 'group of groups' to recurse through.
Leaves and branches genuinely need very different interfaces — forcing them to match hides real differences.
You need to strictly prevent leaf-only operations (like 'add child') from being callable on leaves; the shared interface makes that awkward.
commonMistakes: Putting child-management methods (add/remove) on the shared interface, so leaves are forced to implement (or throw on) operations that make no sense for them.
Forgetting cycle protection — a folder that (accidentally or maliciously) contains itself causes infinite recursion.
Using Composite for a structure that isn't really hierarchical, just to get 'one interface' for unrelated concerns.
Not caching expensive recursive computations (like total size) on large trees, recomputing the whole subtree on every call.
explanation.realWorldExample: The DOM (`Element` nodes containing other nodes, all sharing the `Node` interface), file systems, UI component trees, and org-chart / BOM (bill of materials) structures are classic Composite implementations.

conversation.speaker: Mentor
conversation.message: So a single File pretends to be a tree too?

conversation.speaker: Nestor
conversation.message: Exactly — a File is just a tree with zero children. Give it the same interface as Folder, and every recursive operation stops needing to ask 'which kind am I?'

conversation.speaker: Mentor
conversation.message: What if only Folders should support add()?

conversation.speaker: Nestor
conversation.message: That's my real weakness. Putting add() on the shared interface lets someone call it on a File. Some codebases accept that trade-off; others split a narrower 'Component' interface from a 'Composite' one that only branches implement.

codeBattle.scenario: Your UI framework renders individual widgets (Button, Label) and container widgets (Panel, Form) that hold other widgets, and you want render() to work identically no matter how deep the nesting goes.
codeBattle.question: Which hero should you call?
codeBattle.explanation: Nestor gives every widget the same render() interface, so a single Button and a deeply nested Form both render through the identical recursive call.

quiz.question: What structural problem does Composite solve?
options: Client code has to special-case individual objects versus groups of objects in a tree
Two incompatible interfaces need to work together
An object needs to notify many listeners of changes
A class needs to guarantee only one instance
quiz.answer: Client code has to special-case individual objects versus groups of objects in a tree
quiz.explanation: Composite's entire purpose is eliminating that leaf-vs-branch special-casing by giving both the same interface.

quiz.question: In a file-system Composite, how does a Folder typically implement `getSize()`?
options: By recursively summing `getSize()` across all of its children
By storing a fixed size set at construction time
By delegating to a Singleton size calculator
quiz.answer: By recursively summing `getSize()` across all of its children
quiz.explanation: The composite's implementation of the shared operation is exactly where the recursion happens — leaves just return their own value.

quiz.question: What's a common design tension in Composite?
options: Putting child-management methods (add/remove) on the shared interface forces leaves to support operations that don't make sense for them
Composite cannot be used with recursive functions
Every leaf must contain at least one child
Composite requires a database to track parent-child relationships
quiz.answer: Putting child-management methods (add/remove) on the shared interface forces leaves to support operations that don't make sense for them
quiz.explanation: This is the classic Composite trade-off: interface uniformity versus type safety for leaf-only or branch-only operations.

quiz.question: What real-world structure is a textbook example of Composite?
options: The DOM, where every node (element or text) shares the same base Node interface
A payment gateway with only one implementation
quiz.answer: The DOM, where every node (element or text) shares the same base Node interface
quiz.explanation: The DOM's uniform Node interface across both container and leaf nodes is one of the most widely used real-world Composite implementations.
